title: Generalized Mermin Inequalities for Benchmarking Large-Scale GHZ States
authors: Jianbin Cai, Junxiang Huang, Fynn Otto, Yuan Li, Carlos de Gois, Tao Jiang, Sirui Cao, Fangzheng Chen, Hao Fu, Jin Lin, Wei Xie, Naibin Zhou, Shibiao Tang, Xiang-Yang Li, Cheng-Zhi Peng, Xiao Yuan, Otfried Gühne, Ming Gong
abstract: Multipartite Bell tests provide a correlation-only route to benchmarking quantum processors, but their application at large scales is hindered by the rapid decay of many-body correlators under noise and exponentially many terms in conventional Bell expressions. Here we address these scalability obstacles by introducing a finite-setting generalized Mermin family of state-tailored Bell inequalities with analytic certification bounds, in which the measurement-setting number $m$ provides an additional certification dimension complementary to the system size $n$. We show that, for the powers-of-two setting choices considered here, increasing $m$ leaves the ideal normalized multipartite quantum value unchanged while lowering the relevant classical bounds, thereby strengthening the Bell-violation ratios and yielding an improved noise-robustness scaling compared to the standard Mermin inequality. We test this construction experimentally on a programmable superconducting processor by preparing Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states of up to 80 qubits. Using randomized sampling for direct Bell-operator estimation, we observe Bell ratios that grow exponentially with system size, certify a nonlocality depth of 14, and show that increasing $m$ strengthens both the Bell ratio and depth certification. All results are obtained solely from measured correlators and analytical bounds, without readout correction, tomography, or model-based mitigation. Generalized Mermin inequalities therefore provide a sharper Bell benchmark for noisy large-scale GHZ states.
summary: The paper proposes and experimentally validates generalized Mermin inequalities as an improved benchmark for testing large-scale GHZ states on superconducting processors. By incorporating an extra measurement setting parameter ($m$), the inequality strengthens its violation ratio and certifies a deeper nonlocality depth compared to standard tests. This provides a powerful, noise-robust tool for assessing quantum processor performance using only measured correlations.
main_problem: The primary challenge is benchmarking large-scale quantum processors using multipartite Bell tests, which suffer from noise susceptibility and exponentially complex expressions.
main_result: The authors introduce generalized Mermin inequalities that strengthen the Bell violation ratio and certify a higher nonlocality depth compared to standard methods, even when considering noise.
method: They developed a finite-setting generalized Mermin family of state-tailored Bell inequalities ($\mathcal{M}_{m,n}$) and tested them experimentally using randomized sampling on superconducting qubits.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states prepared on a programmable superconducting processor with up to 80 qubits. The theoretical framework involves generalizing Mermin operators by introducing an additional measurement setting dimension, $m$.
key_observables: Bell violation ratio ($	ext{Did}_{m,n}$), certified nonlocality depth ($k$), and the expectation value of the generalized Mermin operator $\langle\mathcal{M}_{m,n}angle$.
important_parameters: System size $n$ (up to 80 qubits) and measurement setting number $m$ (generalized beyond standard $m=2$).
main_assumptions: The test relies solely on measured correlators and analytical bounds, avoiding readout correction or tomography. The locality and freedom-of-choice loopholes are noted as open.
figures_summary: Figures compare Bell ratios for different settings ($m=2$ vs $m=8$) showing exponential scaling advantages; other figures detail the experimental sequence and the relationship between certified depth and system size.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the generalized Mermin inequality framework, derives analytic bounds comparing it to standard tests, details the experimental implementation on superconducting qubits (including error suppression), presents results showing improved Bell ratios and depth certification with increasing $m$, and concludes by analyzing the hierarchy of local bounds.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses scalability in quantum benchmarking, providing a robust, resource-efficient method to certify nonlocality depth using only measured correlators, which is crucial for near-term noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices.
